pages.text: Ancient Rome

image.note: Cover: the Colosseum, a straight Roman road

pages.text: Contents. From a Village to a Power / The Roman Republic / The Army and the Roads / Life in a Roman City / From Republic to Empire / The Long Fall of Rome.

It began as a huddle of huts on seven hills beside a river. It grew into the greatest empire the western world had ever seen, ruling from the cold edge of Britain to the sands of Egypt. This is the story of Rome: how a small town conquered a world, and then lost it.

image.note: Map: Rome's empire at its height

pages.text: The Romans borrowed much from the Greeks: their gods, their ideas, their art. But the Romans added something of their own. If the Greeks were the great thinkers, the Romans were the great doers: the builders, the soldiers, the rulers who turned ideas into roads, laws, and stone.

chapters.title: From a Village to a Power

pages.text: The Romans loved to tell how their city began. Twin baby brothers, they said, were left to die by a river, and saved and raised by a wolf. One brother, Romulus, later founded a city on the hills and gave it his name: Rome.

That is a legend, of course. The true beginning was humbler: a cluster of villages on seven hills beside the River Tiber, well placed for trade and easy to defend. Slowly the villages joined, and became a town, and the town began to grow.

The Romans were proud and practical people, and they told a proud story of their birth. But they kept the memory of the truth too: that they began as farmers and shepherds on muddy hills, and built the greatest empire on earth not from magic, but from hard work, good sense, and stubbornness.

image.note: Roman farmers on the seven hills

pages.text: For its first centuries, Rome was ruled by kings. But the last kings grew cruel and proud, until the Romans drove them out altogether and swore a mighty oath: never again would one man rule Rome alone.

In place of a king, they built something new. They called it the republic, from words meaning "the public thing", the business of the people. Rome would be governed not by a crown, but by its citizens and their chosen leaders.

Rome's great fear shaped everything it built. Having thrown out its kings, it was terrified of ever handing so much power to one man again. Almost every rule of the republic, two leaders instead of one, short terms, councils to watch each other, was made to stop a single person becoming king. For centuries, it worked.

In the republic, Rome was led by two officials called consuls, elected each year to govern together. Two, so that neither could become a king. And only for a year, so that no one could hold power too long. The Romans feared a single ruler above all things.

Advising them was the Senate, a council of Rome's older and more experienced men, who guided the city's decisions and its wars. Below them, assemblies of citizens voted on laws and chose officials. Rome, like Athens, had learned to share power out.

The Romans had a proud sign for their whole way of doing things: SPQR, standing for the Senate and People of Rome. They stamped it on their coins, their buildings, and the standards their armies carried into battle. It meant: this is not one man's kingdom. This belongs to us all.

The Romans also did something that would shape the world for ever. They wrote their laws down, carved in public for all to read, so that everyone might know the rules, and no judge could simply invent them. Much of the law in your country today grew from Roman roots.

Under the republic, Rome grew hungry and strong. City by city, land by land, it spread across Italy and then beyond, until it ruled the whole of the great inland sea, which the Romans proudly called "our sea".
How did one city conquer so much? The answer, above all, was its army: the most disciplined fighting force the world had yet seen. Rome did not just have brave men. It had a machine.

Roman soldiers, the legionaries, trained relentlessly and fought as one. They locked their shields into walls and even roofs of iron, and moved together like a single beast. A Roman army that lost a battle would simply come back, and back, and back, until it won.

A Roman soldier was a walking city. He carried not just his sword and shield but tools, cooking pots, food, and stakes for a fort, often thirty kilos or more, marching thirty kilometres a day. Every single night on the march the army built a fortified camp, and every morning they took it down again.

But the legions did more than fight. Wherever they conquered, they built. Bridges. Forts. And above all, roads: long, straight, beautifully made roads, running arrow-straight over hill and marsh, so soldiers and messages could move fast across the empire.
These roads were so well made that some are still walked on today, two thousand years later. They tied the whole empire together, and gave us a saying we still use: all roads lead to Rome.

The Romans were master builders in everything. They discovered a kind of concrete so strong it has lasted millennia. They raised aqueducts, stone channels on soaring arches, to carry fresh water for many miles into their cities. Where Rome ruled, clean water flowed.

Think of the cleverness of an aqueduct. To keep the water flowing, it had to fall ever so gently downhill for its whole length, sometimes sixty kilometres or more, dropping just a few centimetres every hundred paces. Get it wrong, and the water would stop, or flood. The Romans got it right, again and again, without a single machine.

image.note: Aqueduct arches marching across a valley

pages.text: To be a Roman was to live in a city grander than almost anywhere on earth. Rome itself held perhaps a million people, packed into apartment blocks, temples, and markets, fed by grain from across the sea.

Romans loved their public baths, vast halls of warm and cold pools where people washed, exercised, and met their friends. A trip to the baths was less about getting clean and more about spending the whole afternoon among the whole city.

A Roman child's day might start at school before dawn, chalk and wax tablet in hand, chanting lessons aloud. Boys, and some girls, learned reading, writing, and sums. Lessons were long and strict, and a lazy pupil could expect the cane. Roman school was no holiday.

image.note: Roman children at lessons with wax tablets

pages.text: Water ran to public fountains and even to some homes. Beneath the streets ran drains to carry the dirty water away. In their comfort and their engineering, Roman cities would not be matched again in Europe for over a thousand years after Rome fell.

For entertainment, Romans flocked to the games. In great arenas like the Colosseum, tens of thousands watched races, contests, and fights between trained warriors called gladiators. It was thrilling, and often cruel, and the crowds adored it.

The Romans went to enormous lengths to thrill the crowds. They could even flood an arena with water and stage mock sea-battles in the middle of the city. Free bread was handed out, and free entry, so that even the poorest Romans were kept fed and entertained. "Bread and games," some grumbled, was how Rome kept its people quiet.

image.note: Arena flooded for a mock sea-battle

pages.text: Not all Romans shared this good life. The comfort of the city rested on the labour of countless enslaved people, who had no freedom and no choice, and on the grain and gold taken from conquered lands. Rome's glory had a hard and unjust price.

image.note: A quiet, honest note: workers unseen

pages.text: Still, for a citizen, the Roman world offered roads to travel safely, laws to appeal to, cities to trade in, and a single language, Latin, understood from Britain to the desert. For a while, a huge and peaceful world lay open under one great name.

image.note: Traveller on a safe imperial road

pages.text: One Roman town gives us our clearest window of all into daily life, because of a terrible day. The town was Pompeii, and it sat in the shadow of a mountain that everyone thought was just a hill. That mountain was a sleeping volcano, and one afternoon it woke.

In a single day, the volcano buried Pompeii deep under ash. It was a disaster for the people who lived there. But the ash also sealed the town like a time capsule, and kept it safe for nearly two thousand years.

image.note: Ash falling over the town, people fleeing

pages.text: When the town was dug up again, long after, people found Rome frozen in an instant. Loaves of bread still in the ovens. Pots on the tables. Jokes and messages scratched on the walls. Pompeii lets us walk into a Roman street and see, better than any book, exactly how Romans lived.

image.note: Excavated Pompeii street, bread and pots

pages.text: As Rome grew vast, its old republic began to strain. Generals who conquered new lands came home rich, famous, and commanding armies loyal to them rather than to Rome. The city that feared kings now bred men mightier than any king.

The most famous was Julius Caesar, a brilliant and ambitious general who conquered new lands and won the love of his soldiers and the common people. Many Romans cheered him. But others feared he wished to make himself a king, and so break their most ancient oath.

There was a moment everyone remembers. Caesar's enemies ordered him to give up his army and come home alone. Instead, he marched his soldiers across a small border river called the Rubicon, which the law forbade, and by crossing it began a war. Ever since, to cross the Rubicon has meant to take a step you can never take back.

image.note: Caesar's army crossing a small river

pages.text: Their fear ran so deep that a group of senators turned on Caesar and killed him, in the Senate itself, hoping to save the republic. Instead, they destroyed it. Rome fell into years of civil war, Roman against Roman.

Out of that chaos rose Caesar's heir, a cool and cunning young man who defeated all his rivals and took sole power. He was careful never to call himself king. He called himself the first citizen. But he ruled alone, and took a new title: Augustus, the first Roman emperor.

Augustus was clever enough never to wear a crown or take the name of king. He kept the Senate, kept the old titles, and let Rome feel as though nothing had changed. But every real decision was now his. He proved that the surest way to hold total power can be to make it look as though you have none.

The republic was over. Rome was now ruled by emperors, one man at the top, exactly what its founders had sworn to prevent. Yet under the early emperors, Rome reached its greatest size and a long stretch of peace. The empire was born from the death of the republic.

image.note: Empire at its peak, one throne

pages.text: No empire in this world lasts for ever, and Rome was no exception, though it took a very long time to fall. For centuries it stood, so vast that in time it split into two halves, east and west, each with its own ruler, simply so that it could be governed at all.

The western half slowly weakened. It grew too big to defend. Its borders were long and its enemies were many. Money ran short, rulers rose and fell, and peoples from beyond the frontier pushed in, some to raid, some simply seeking a home.

There was no single day when Rome "fell". It faded, over long years, until the last western emperor quietly lost his throne, and the great machine of the west finally fell still. The city that had ruled the world was ruled now by others.

But remember the eastern half. It did not fall. It lived on for another thousand years as the empire we met in another book, with its capital at Constantinople. Half of Rome died. Half of Rome refused to.

image.note: Map: west dark, east still glowing

pages.text: And even where it fell, Rome never truly vanished. Its roads still run. Its laws live inside our own. Its language became the parent of Spanish, French, Italian, and thousands of English words. Its calendar hangs on your wall, its months still bearing Roman names.

image.note: Roman echoes in the modern world

pages.text: So look around you. The very letters on this page were shaped by Rome. Our months July and August are named for Roman rulers. The idea of laws that apply to everyone is theirs. An empire can fall, and still quietly run the world two thousand years later.

A village on seven hills grew to rule the world, and then let it slip away. But it left the world so changed that, two thousand years on, you still live among the works and the words of Rome, and may not even know it.

image.note: Modern city with Roman bones beneath

pages.text: Words to know. Republic: a state without a king, led by chosen officials. Consul: one of two yearly leaders. Senate: Rome's council of elders. Legion: a large unit of the Roman army. Aqueduct: a channel carrying water. Emperor: the sole ruler of an empire.
Rome borrowed from Greece and passed its gifts to us. But halfway across the world, other empires rose that Rome never dreamed of. There is always another story over the next hill. Where will you go?
